title: Clauses: Main, Subordinate and Their Functions

blocks.text: "Abeokuta is the town where my grandmother was born." Most candidates see *where* and answer "adverbial clause of place". They lose the mark. The clause does not say where anything happened — it says which town. The introducing word never decides the answer; the job the clause does decides it.

blocks.title: Clause
blocks.text: A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb. A main (independent) clause makes complete sense alone. A subordinate (dependent) clause has a subject and finite verb too, but a subordinator in front of it leaves it needing the rest of the sentence.

blocks.markdown:
### Step one: main or subordinate?

Read the clause aloud on its own.

- *the lorry took the longer route* — complete in itself → **main clause**
- *because the road was flooded* — leaves you waiting → **subordinate clause**

The word that makes a clause subordinate is either a **subordinating conjunction** (because, although, if, when, until, since, unless, so that, as soon as) or a **relative pronoun** (who, whom, whose, which, that) or a **relative adverb** (when, where, why).

### Step two: which of the three jobs?

Every subordinate clause does one of exactly three jobs.

**Noun clause** — fills a slot a noun could fill. Test by substituting *it* or *something*.
> **What the witness said** surprised the court. (subject)
> Everyone knows **that the fees were increased**. (object)
> The panel awarded it to **whoever bid lowest**. (object of a preposition)

**Adjectival clause** — tells you *which one*, and sits beside the noun it describes.
> The bridge **that the contractor repaired** collapsed.
> Abeokuta is the town **where my grandmother was born**.

**Adverbial clause** — modifies the verb, answering when, where, why, how, on what condition or in spite of what.
> The farmers planted **as soon as the first rains fell**.

blocks.title: Classifying a clause the reliable way
blocks.prompt: State the function of the underlined clause: "Abeokuta is the town **where my grandmother was born**."

steps.text: Check that it is a clause. It has the subject *my grandmother* and the finite verb *was born*, so yes.
Check that it is subordinate. *Where* opens it and it cannot stand alone, so it is subordinate.
Resist the introducing word. Do not decide from *where*; ask what the clause is doing.
Try the noun test: substitute *it*. 'Abeokuta is the town it' is nonsense, so it is not a noun clause.
Try the adjectival test: does it tell you which one? 'Which town? The one where my grandmother was born.' Yes — it identifies *town*.
Confirm by contrast: in 'She sat where the shade was thickest', the same word *where* opens a clause that modifies the verb *sat*, and that one is adverbial of place.

blocks.answer: An adjectival (relative) clause modifying the noun *town*

items: Confirm the group is a clause by finding a subject and a finite verb.
Decide main or subordinate by reading it alone.
For a subordinate clause, substitute *it* — if the sentence still works, it is a noun clause.
If it answers *which one* about a nearby noun, it is adjectival.
If it answers when, where, why, how, on what condition or in spite of what, it is adverbial.
Name the sub-type using the question it answers, not the word that introduces it.

blocks.title: *When* and *where* are ambiguous
blocks.text: These two words open adjectival clauses when they follow a noun of time or place — *the day when we met*, *the town where she was born* — and adverbial clauses when they modify a verb — *we left when the rain stopped*. Always check what the clause is attached to.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: In the exam the question is usually phrased "the function of the clause is". Answer in the form 'noun clause acting as object of ...' or 'adjectival clause modifying ...' or 'adverbial clause of time'. Naming both the type and what it attaches to earns the full mark.

points: Every clause has a subject and a finite verb; only a main clause can stand alone.
Subordinators, relative pronouns and relative adverbs make a clause dependent.
Subordinate clauses do one of three jobs: noun, adjectival or adverbial.
Substitute *it* to test for a noun clause; ask *which one* to test for an adjectival clause.
Name an adverbial clause by the question it answers, not by the word that introduces it.
*When* and *where* can open either an adjectival or an adverbial clause, so check what they attach to.
